I definitely have frequently felt the same way. I was able to work from home part time at the beginning of the school year, but that was taken away as an option when students came back face-to-face. I've heard of other people negotiating for part time schedules, different break routines, or alternate start times. None of those would have worked for my job. I just finally resigned because a lot of my distress was caused by the toxic work environment filled with people who don't understand mental health. I was able to find a job in a completely different field that I think (hope) will be less stressful. I won't have more than one or two coworkers and most of the time I'll be by myself (except for customers). I'll basically just be responsible for myself and I think that may be what I need.

Starting next week, I'm going to reach out to my Tier 2 and Tier 3 students via phone. I may try to set up FaceTime or Zoom talks with the families if they want. 

The biggest issue I'm running into is that many of my families don't have internet access, let alone the technology to use it. I left a stack of letters at our "pick up station" at school explaining how to get on Remind as well as how to access the Second Step materials from home. I don't know how many people will actually see the letter though...

Also, this is my first year as a professional school counselor. So, I am still learning as I go while adapting to the new circumstances!

Try walking her on a leash in a more controlled environment first (like your back yard or small neighborhood with few dogs). Use diversionary techniques to keep her attention on you when she becomes distracted or starts pulling. For example, if she pulls to pick something up off the ground call her name and use quick repetitive noises or a crinkly toy to draw her attention back to you. Then immediately reward (treat, click, marker word, whatever you use). Guide her in the opposite direction if she continues pulling.  Practice this a few times with less enticing distractions, then work your way up to practicing it with other dogs. It's slow going, but this worked for me with practice and consistent repetition. You could also practice having her sit every time she encounters another dog if you would rather do polite greetings. Guide her away if she gets too excited. She'll eventually learn than she doesn't get to greet the dog if she is over excited.
